\section[dirigirse]{dirigirse — to head (for), to make your way; to speak to}

\label{lesson:ES-C673-dirigirse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the signs, then the Spanish for the diversion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dirigirse}
\textbf{dirigirse} — \textquotedblleft{}to head (for), to make your way; to speak to\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nos dirigimos a la salida.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We are heading for the exit.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Dirigirse a alguien} — to address someone. The g becomes j: \emph{me dirijo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dirigirse} is built on \emph{dirigir}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{dīrigere} \textquotedblleft{}to lay straight, to direct\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dirigirse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dirigirse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{dirigirse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the signs, then the Spanish for the diversion, then say \emph{dirigirse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does dirigirse mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To head (for), to make your way; to speak to\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acortar]{acortar — to shorten; to cut short}

\label{lesson:ES-C673-acortar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the diversion, then the Spanish for to head.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acortar}
\textbf{acortar} — \textquotedblleft{}to shorten; to cut short\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Por el parque acortamos camino.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Going through the park shortens the way.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Acortar camino} — to take a short cut; \emph{el atajo} is the short cut itself.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{acortar} is built on \emph{corto} \textquotedblleft{}short\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{curtus} \textquotedblleft{}shortened, incomplete\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); EtymDB also links it with \emph{cortar} \textquotedblleft{}to cut\textquotedblright{}, from the same Latin word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{acortar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{acortar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{acortar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the diversion, then the Spanish for to head, then say \emph{acortar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does acortar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To shorten; to cut short\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[retroceder]{retroceder — to go back, to back up}

\label{lesson:ES-C673-retroceder}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to head, then the Spanish for to shorten.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: retroceder}
\textbf{retroceder} — \textquotedblleft{}to go back, to back up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tuvimos que retroceder dos kilómetros.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We had to go back two kilometres.}
\end{quote}

In a car, \emph{dar marcha atrás} is to reverse.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{retroceder} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{retrōcēdere} \textquotedblleft{}to go back, to retire\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB), from \emph{retrō} \textquotedblleft{}back\textquotedblright{} and \emph{cēdere} \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{retroceder}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{retroceder}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{retroceder}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to head, then the Spanish for to shorten, then say \emph{retroceder} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does retroceder mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To go back, to back up\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[rodear]{rodear — to go round; to surround}

\label{lesson:ES-C673-rodear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to shorten, then the Spanish for to go back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rodear}
\textbf{rodear} — \textquotedblleft{}to go round; to surround\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Rodeamos el lago a pie.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We walked round the lake.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Rodeado de} — surrounded by.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rodear} is built on \emph{rueda} \textquotedblleft{}wheel\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{rota}: to go round as a wheel does.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{rodear}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to shorten, then the Spanish for to go back, then say \emph{rodear} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[bordear]{bordear — to go along the edge of, to skirt}

\label{lesson:ES-C673-bordear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to go back, then the Spanish for to go round.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bordear}
\textbf{bordear} — \textquotedblleft{}to go along the edge of, to skirt\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El camino bordea la costa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The path runs along the coast.}
\end{quote}

Close to \emph{rodear}, but along the edge rather than all the way round.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{bordear} is built on \emph{borde} \textquotedblleft{}edge\textquotedblright{}, which came from French \emph{bord} (EtymDB), a word of Germanic origin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to go back, then the Spanish for to go round, then say \emph{bordear} again
